questions.q: What does RPO (Recovery Point Objective) actually measure?
options: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured in time
The maximum acceptable amount of downtime, measured in time
The total storage cost of a disaster recovery solution
The number of replicas a database must have
questions.explain: RPO answers "how much data are we willing to lose?" — expressed as a span of time, like "at most 15 minutes."

questions.q: What does RTO (Recovery Time Objective) actually measure?
options: The maximum acceptable amount of downtime before the system is back
The maximum acceptable amount of data loss
How often full backups should be scheduled
The geographic distance required between primary and secondary regions
questions.explain: RTO answers "how long can we be down?" — a business tolerance for downtime, not a technical setting.

questions.q: Per this lesson, in what order should RPO/RTO and technology choice happen?
options: Ask the business for real tolerances first, write down RPO/RTO as explicit numbers, and only then choose a technology capable of hitting them
Pick the most advanced-sounding HA/DR technology first, then report whatever RPO/RTO it happens to deliver
Skip RPO/RTO entirely and rely on the DBA's personal judgment
Ask the business only after the technology is already in production
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly calls picking technology first and backing into RPO/RTO backwards — business requirements come first.

questions.q: Given the requirement "can't lose more than a few minutes of orders, back within 30 minutes," what RPO/RTO does that convert to?
options: RPO = 5 minutes, RTO = 30 minutes
RPO = 24 hours, RTO = 24 hours
RPO = 30 minutes, RTO = 5 minutes
There is no way to convert a business statement into numbers
questions.explain: "A few minutes of data loss" becomes an RPO of about 5 minutes, and "back within 30 minutes" becomes an RTO of 30 minutes.

questions.q: Why can a nightly-backup-only strategy never satisfy an RPO of 5 minutes?
options: Because the RPO can never be tighter than the backup/replication frequency feeding it — nightly backups alone give roughly a 24-hour RPO at best
Because nightly backups are always corrupted
Because RPO has nothing to do with backup frequency
Because Azure SQL does not support nightly backups
questions.explain: RPO is bounded by how often data is actually captured — log backups or continuous replication are required to hit a tight RPO like 5 minutes.
